questions.prompt: In a class body: xs = [1, 2]; k = 3; zs = [x * k for x in xs]. What happens on Python 3.11?
options: NameError for k, because the comprehension scope cannot see class-level names; only the leftmost iterable xs is read in the class scope
NameError for xs, because comprehensions cannot read any class-level names
It works and gives [3, 6], because class variables are visible in nested scopes
It works but gives [1, 2], because k is looked up as a global default of 1
questions.explanation: The leftmost iterable (xs) is evaluated in the enclosing class scope, so xs is found. The element expression x * k runs in the implicit comprehension function, and a class block's names are not visible to nested scopes (Execution model, resolution of names), so k raises NameError: name 'k' is not defined. Fixes: build the list outside the class, or iterate over pairs such as itertools.product so that the value arrives through the leftmost iterable.

questions.skillLabel: Memo cache stored in a default argument
questions.prompt: def fib(n, memo={}): calls += 1; if n < 2: return n; if n not in memo: memo[n] = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2); return memo[n] (calls counts every invocation; the recursive calls do not pass memo). How many invocations does the first call fib(20) make? Give the number.
questions.explanation: The recursive calls use the shared default dict. Let T(n) be the invocations of a cold-memo call fib(n). T(2) = 3 (fib(2), fib(1), fib(0)). For n >= 3, fib(n) calls fib(n-1), which costs T(n-1) and fills memo for every smaller index from 2, and then fib(n-2), which is already in memo (or is a base case) and costs exactly 1 invocation: T(n) = 1 + T(n-1) + 1 = T(n-1) + 2. Hence T(n) = 2n - 1 and T(20) = 39 (confirmed by running the code on Python 3.11.9). A second call fib(20) takes 1 invocation because the memo persists in fib.__defaults__, and the version without memo makes 21891 invocations.

questions.skillLabel: Deep copy memo and aliasing structure
questions.prompt: For a = [7, 8] and s = [a, a], what are d[0] is d[1] and d[0] is a for d = copy.deepcopy(s)? Explain how the memo dictionary produces this, why a self-referential list x = [1]; x.append(x) does not make deepcopy loop forever, and how to make two separate deepcopy calls share a copy of a.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided. Model answer: d[0] is d[1] is True and d[0] is a is False. deepcopy keeps a memo mapping id(original) to its copy for the current call; the first time it meets a it copies it and records the copy, the second time it finds a in the memo and returns the same copy, so the aliasing pattern of s is reproduced while a itself is duplicated. For x it registers the new list in the memo before copying its items, so when it reaches x again inside itself it returns the new list: the result y satisfies y is not x and y[1] is y. The memo lives for one call; to share copies between calls pass the same dict, e.g. m = {}; c1 = copy.deepcopy(t1, m); c2 = copy.deepcopy(t2, m), after which c1[0] is c2[0].
rubric: States d[0] is d[1] is True and d[0] is a is False.
Explains the memo as a mapping from id(original) to the copy, consulted before copying and reused on the second encounter.
Explains that the copy is registered before descending, so the cycle maps back to the new list: y is not x and y[1] is y.
Says the memo lasts only for one call and shows passing a shared memo dict to two calls.
